blocks.text: Before you can understand embeddings, gradients, or how a neural network multiplies numbers together, you need three building blocks that everything else in AI math is built from: scalars, vectors, and matrices. They sound abstract, but you already use versions of all three in everyday life. This lesson builds each one up from scratch, with real examples pulled straight from AI work, and then shows exactly how the three fit together inside a real neural network.

blocks.alt: A ladder diagram showing scalar leading to vector leading to matrix leading to tensor
blocks.caption: The whole lesson in one picture: each structure is built by arranging the previous one.

blocks.text: 1. What Is a Scalar?

A scalar is just a single number. Nothing more. No direction, no list, no structure attached to it. If someone asks "how much" or "how many" and the answer is one plain number, that number is a scalar.

items: A temperature reading, like 21 degrees.
A learning rate, like 0.001.
The number of layers in a neural network, like 12.
A loss value at one single training step, like 0.734.

code.content:
learning_rate = 0.001   # scalar
num_epochs = 50          # scalar
loss = 0.734             # scalar

blocks.text: In tensor libraries like NumPy or PyTorch, a scalar is described as a 0-dimensional array, written as shape = (). Zero dimensions simply means there is nothing to index into, it is just one value sitting by itself. Every other structure in this lesson is built by arranging scalars together in some organized way.
2. What Is a Vector?

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, a 1-dimensional array. The word "ordered" matters a lot here: [2, 5, 1] and [5, 2, 1] contain the exact same three numbers, but they are not the same vector, because the position of each number carries meaning.

items: A word embedding is a vector, for example a 768-number list that represents the meaning of one single word.
A row of tabular data, like age, income, and years of experience, is a vector.
The weights feeding into one neuron of a neural network are a vector.

code.content:
import numpy as np

embedding = np.array([0.12, -0.48, 0.91, 0.03])
print(embedding.shape)   # (4,)  a 1-D vector with 4 numbers in it

blocks.text: The dimension of a vector is just how many numbers it holds, nothing more mysterious than that. Real embedding models typically use vectors with hundreds or thousands of dimensions. The 4-number vector above is small on purpose, just to make it easy to look at.

blocks.title: A quick mental picture
blocks.content: Think of a vector as a single row in a spreadsheet. Each column holds one number, the order of the columns is fixed, and the whole row together describes one thing, whether that thing is a word, a customer, or a training example.

blocks.text: It is worth noticing that a scalar and a vector of length 1, like [5], are not quite the same thing either, even though they hold the same single number. A scalar has shape (), truly zero-dimensional, while a length-1 vector has shape (1,), one dimension that just happens to hold one item. Code that expects one and receives the other is a common, if minor, source of confusion.
3. What Is a Matrix?

A matrix is a 2-dimensional grid of numbers, arranged in rows and columns. One useful way to picture it: a matrix is a stack of vectors. A batch of 3 word embeddings, each one 4 numbers long, is a 3 by 4 matrix, 3 rows and 4 columns.

blocks.alt: A 3 by 4 matrix, 3 rows and 4 columns, each cell holding one number
blocks.caption: Each row here is one full embedding vector; each column is the same position across every embedding.

code.content:
batch = np.array([
    [0.12, -0.48, 0.91, 0.03],    # embedding for word 1
    [0.55,  0.02, -0.31, 0.77],   # embedding for word 2
    [-0.09, 0.64,  0.18, -0.22],  # embedding for word 3
])
print(batch.shape)   # (3, 4)  3 rows, 4 columns

blocks.text: This is exactly why matrices matter so much in AI engineering. A whole batch of training examples, an entire set of weights connecting one layer to the next, the attention score between every pair of tokens in a sentence, all of it gets stored and processed as a matrix, because GPUs are built to do matrix math extremely fast.
3.1 A Vector Is Really Just a Special Matrix

Formally, a vector is a matrix that happens to have only one row, or only one column. There is no separate rulebook for vectors, they are simply the special case of a matrix where one of the two dimensions equals 1. This is why a row vector has shape (1, 4) and a column vector has shape (4, 1), both introduced earlier in this lesson, they are matrices in every technical sense.

code.content:
row_vector = np.array([[4, 3]])      # shape (1, 2), a 1-row matrix
col_vector = np.array([[4], [3]])    # shape (2, 1), a 1-column matrix

blocks.text: This is also why some libraries let a plain shape (4,) vector and a shape (1, 4) row vector be used almost interchangeably in many operations, while other operations are strict about the difference. When in doubt, printing .shape before and after an operation is the fastest way to confirm which one you are actually holding.
3.2 Transpose: Flipping Rows and Columns

One operation you will use constantly on a matrix is the transpose, which flips every row into a column and every column into a row. A 2 by 3 matrix becomes a 3 by 2 matrix, and the number that used to sit at row i, column j now sits at row j, column i.

blocks.alt: A 2 by 3 matrix and its transpose, a 3 by 2 matrix, with rows and columns swapped
blocks.caption: Every row of the original becomes a column of the transpose, in the same order.

blocks.text: Transpose gets its own full lesson later in this module, but it is worth introducing now because it comes up immediately once matrix multiplication and dot products enter the picture, both of which frequently need one of the two matrices flipped first for the shapes to line up correctly.
4. Indexing and Slicing

Once numbers are arranged into a vector or a matrix, you need a way to pull individual pieces back out. This works the same way for both, you just need one position for a vector and two positions, row and column, for a matrix.

code.content:
v = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(v[0])    # 10, the first number
print(v[-1])   # 40, the last number

blocks.alt: A matrix with its second row highlighted in blue and its third column highlighted in red
blocks.caption: The colon in M[1, :] means every column of that row; the colon in M[:, 2] means every row of that column.

blocks.text: Counting starts at 0, not 1, in Python and NumPy. That means the "2nd row" a person would point at is stored at index 1, and the "3rd column" is stored at index 2. This trips up almost everyone the first time, so it is worth reading twice.

Negative indices work on matrices too, not just vectors. M[-1, :] fetches the last row, and M[:, -1] fetches the last column, which is a convenient shortcut whenever you do not know or do not care exactly how many rows or columns the matrix has.
5. Row Vectors vs Column Vectors

A plain vector like [4, 3] has shape (2,), and NumPy treats it as neither a row nor a column, just a flat list. Sometimes, especially before a matrix multiplication, code needs to be explicit about orientation: a row vector has shape (1, 2), one row and two columns, and a column vector has shape (2, 1), two rows and one column.

code.content:
v = np.array([4, 3])
print(v.shape)                  # (2,)

row = v.reshape(1, 2)
print(row.shape)                # (1, 2)

col = v.reshape(2, 1)
print(col.shape)                # (2, 1)

blocks.title: Why this is worth knowing early
blocks.content: The same two numbers, 4 and 3, can be stored as shape (2,), (1, 2), or (2, 1), and these are not interchangeable once matrix multiplication is involved later in this module. A shape mismatch is one of the single most common errors in real AI code, and it almost always traces back to exactly this row-versus-column confusion.

blocks.text: 5.1 Special Matrices You Will See Constantly
A handful of specific matrices show up so often in AI code that it helps to recognize them by name on sight.

items: Identity matrix: 1s down the diagonal, 0s everywhere else, it is the matrix equivalent of multiplying by 1, leaving anything it multiplies unchanged.
Zero matrix: every single entry is 0, the matrix equivalent of the number 0.
Diagonal matrix: numbers only along the diagonal, 0s everywhere else, often used to represent independent scaling along each axis.

blocks.text: 6. Putting Them Together: Inside a Neural Network Layer

Here is where scalars, vectors, and matrices stop being separate ideas and start working as a team. A single layer of a neural network takes an input vector, multiplies it by a weight matrix, adds a bias vector, and produces an output vector. Every one of the three structures from this lesson shows up in that one sentence.

blocks.alt: A flow diagram showing an input vector going through a weight matrix multiply plus bias, producing an output vector
blocks.caption: One layer of a neural network, expressed entirely in the vocabulary from this lesson.

code.content:
x = np.array([2, 1])              # input vector, shape (2,)
W = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])    # weight matrix, shape (2, 2)
b = np.array([0.5, -0.5])         # bias vector, shape (2,)

y = W.dot(x) + b
print(y)   # [2.5, 0.5]  the output vector

blocks.text: Each individual number inside W, each individual number inside x, and the final loss computed later from y, are all scalars. The rows of W are vectors. And W itself, holding every one of those rows together, is the matrix. This is not a separate topic from what came before, it is the same three ideas, just doing real work.
6.1 Chaining Two Layers Together

Real neural networks stack many layers, and the output vector of one layer becomes the input vector of the next. Extending the single-layer example from above by one more layer shows exactly how that chain works.

code.content:
x = np.array([2, 1])                  # input vector
W1 = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])       # layer 1 weights
b1 = np.array([0.5, -0.5])
h = W1.dot(x) + b1                    # [2.5, 0.5], output of layer 1

W2 = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 2]])       # layer 2 weights
b2 = np.array([0, 0])
y = W2.dot(h) + b2                    # [5.0, 1.0], final output
print(y)

blocks.text: Notice that h, the output of the first layer, is used directly as the input vector to the second layer matrix multiplication. This is the entire idea behind a deep network: the exact same vector-times-matrix-plus-vector pattern repeated over and over, each time producing a new vector that feeds the next layer.

blocks.alt: A flow diagram showing an input vector passing through layer 1 into a hidden vector, then through layer 2 into an output vector
blocks.caption: The hidden vector h is the bridge, it is the output of layer 1 and the input of layer 2 at the same time.

blocks.text: This chaining is exactly why deep networks are called deep, each additional layer is one more link in this same chain, every one of them a vector passing through a matrix multiply and a bias add.
7. Scalar vs Vector vs Matrix, Side by Side

blocks.text: One level up from a matrix is a tensor, anything with 3 or more dimensions, like a batch of images described as batch by height by width by color channel. Tensors get covered properly in the Deep Learning section. For now, the ladder scalar to vector to matrix is the exact foundation everything else in Math and Statistics builds on.
7.1 Tensors in the Real World

To make the earlier one-sentence mention of tensors more concrete: a single color image is usually stored as a 3-dimensional tensor, height by width by color channel. A batch of images for training adds one more dimension on top, batch size by height by width by channel, a 4-dimensional tensor.

code.content:
# 32 images, each 224 by 224 pixels, 3 color channels
batch_of_images = np.zeros((32, 224, 224, 3))
print(batch_of_images.shape)   # (32, 224, 224, 3)

blocks.text: The scalar to vector to matrix ladder from this lesson simply keeps extending: a tensor is just what you call the structure once there are 3 or more dimensions involved, with the exact same indexing and broadcasting rules from earlier in this lesson still applying underneath.
8. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming (4,), (1, 4), and (4, 1) are all the same thing, they are not, and mixing them up is a frequent source of shape errors.
Forgetting that changing the order of numbers inside a vector changes what that vector actually represents.
Mixing up rows and columns when reading M[i, j], remembering row comes first and column comes second helps.
Forgetting that counting starts at 0, so the "5th row" is stored at index 4, not index 5.

blocks.text: 9. A Quick Way to Tell Them Apart
Whenever you are not sure which of the three something is, ask one question: how many numbers does it take to describe this one thing, and are those numbers arranged in a line or a grid?

items: One number by itself, with nothing else attached: that is a scalar.
A single ordered list of numbers describing one thing: that is a vector.
Several vectors stacked together into rows and columns: that is a matrix.

blocks.text: 9.1 Practice: Identify the Structure
Before moving on, try classifying each of these as a scalar, a vector, or a matrix, then check the answer underneath.

items: The current temperature of a server, 42.5 degrees.
A user profile made of age, height, and weight.
A spreadsheet of 100 users, each with age, height, and weight.
The similarity score between two documents, 0.87.

blocks.title: Answers
blocks.content: Server temperature: scalar, one plain number. User profile: vector, an ordered list of three numbers describing one user. Spreadsheet of 100 users: matrix, 100 rows, 3 columns. Similarity score: scalar, again a single plain number, even though it was computed by comparing two vectors.

blocks.text: 10. Scalars Acting on Vectors and Matrices

One more combination shows up constantly: a scalar multiplying an entire vector or matrix at once. NumPy applies the scalar to every single number inside the structure, a behavior called broadcasting.

code.content:
v = np.array([4, 3])
print(2 * v)     # [8, 6]  every number doubled

M = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(0.1 * M)   # [[0.1, 0.2], [0.3, 0.4]]  every number scaled by 0.1

blocks.text: This exact pattern is how a learning rate scales a gradient before it updates a model weights, and how an embedding gets rescaled during normalization, covered properly in the magnitude and unit vector lessons. A single scalar reaching in and touching every number in a much bigger structure is one of the most common operations in all of AI training.
11. Why This Foundation Matters Going Forward

Nearly every remaining lesson in this Math and Statistics module leans directly on the three ideas from this one. Distance and similarity are computed between vectors. Matrix multiplication, inverses, and eigenvalues are all properties of matrices. Even topics that sound unrelated, like probability distributions or gradient descent, get expressed using vectors and matrices the moment they are implemented in real code.

Spending the time to get comfortable with shapes, indexing, and the mental picture of scalar, vector, and matrix now pays off on every single lesson that follows, since none of them will stop to re-explain these basics again.
Key Takeaway

A scalar is one number. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, one-dimensional. A matrix is a grid of numbers, two-dimensional, and a good way to picture it is as a stack of vectors. None of this is abstract math for its own sake either: a word embedding is a vector, a batch of embeddings is a matrix, and the weights inside a neural network are stored as matrices too, as the layer example above showed directly.

Order matters for a vector, and rows versus columns matter for a matrix, since the position of each number is part of what it means. Everything else covered later in this Math and Statistics module, distances, dot products, matrix multiplication, builds directly on these three ideas, so it is worth being genuinely comfortable with them before moving on.
